desc:
You are given an array nums of positive integers. For each index i, imagine deleting the element nums[i] (only that one) and looking at the remaining n - 1 elements. Index i is removable if those remaining elements can be split into two groups with exactly the same sum, where every remaining element goes into exactly one of the two groups.

Return the number of removable indices. Equal values at different indices are counted separately.

[2, 2, 2]    -> 3   (any removal leaves [2, 2])
[1, 1, 2]    -> 1   (only removing the 2 leaves [1, 1]; removing a 1 leaves [1, 2])
[1, 2, 3]    -> 0   (no remaining pair has equal parts)
[1, 1, 2, 4] -> 1   (removing 4 leaves [1, 1, 2] = 2 + 2)
hints: For one fixed index the question is exactly Partition Equal Subset Sum. Doing that from scratch for every index is correct, just slow. Can you share work between indices?

Removing element i only matters if the sum of the rest is even; then you need a subset of the other elements with sum equal to half of it. So you need "is sum s reachable using all elements except i".

Divide and conquer on the index range: to answer for all i in [l, r), first add the elements of one half to the reachable-sum set, then recurse into the other half, and the other way round. Each element is added O(log n) times in total.
editorial: For a fixed index i the remaining sum is S - nums[i]. If that is odd the index is not removable. Otherwise we need a subset of the other elements with sum exactly (S - nums[i]) / 2: the standard subset-sum DP. Running it separately for each index costs O(n2 · S).

The shared work can be recovered with a "delete one element" divide and conquer. Define solve(l, r, reach), where reach is the set of sums achievable using all elements outside the range [l, r). If r - l == 1, the set is exactly the set of sums available without element l, and we test the target there. Otherwise split the range at mid: for the left half, add the elements of [mid, r) to reach and recurse; for the right half, add the elements of [l, mid) and recurse. Every element is inserted into a sum-set once per recursion level, so the total number of insertions is O(n log n) and the time is O(n log n · S) (or O(n log n · S / 64) with bitsets).
Only sums up to S / 2 are ever needed, which halves the table. With the limits here (S ≤ 10,000) the divide-and-conquer version needs roughly 200 · 8 · 5,000 = 8 million basic steps.
solution:
def countRemovableElements(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    total = sum(nums)
    limit = total // 2
    mask = (1 << (limit + 1)) - 1
    answer = 0

    def solve(lo, hi, bits):
        # bits: sums reachable using only elements outside [lo, hi)
        nonlocal answer
        if hi - lo == 1:
            rest = total - nums[lo]
            if rest % 2 == 0 and (bits >> (rest // 2)) & 1:
                answer += 1
            return
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        left = bits
        for x in nums[mid:hi]:
            left |= left << x
        solve(lo, mid, left & mask)
        right = bits
        for x in nums[lo:mid]:
            right |= right << x
        solve(mid, hi, right & mask)

    solve(0, n, 1)
    return answer
